name: Transcutaneous hair removal

card.summary: Transcutaneous hair removal refers to skin-surface electrical devices sold for home use that aim to reduce hair for a smoother look without inserting a needle.
card.note: Marketed permanence claims lack published clinical data.

quick.overview:
Transcutaneous hair removal describes devices that apply electrical current through electrodes on the skin surface, rather than a needle in the follicle, with the aim of reducing unwanted facial or body hair. The appearance payoff sought is smooth, hair-free skin without clinic visits.

It is modelled on galvanic electrolysis, in which current produces sodium hydroxide at the follicle that damages hair-growing cells. Wikipedia lists the approach among "doubtful methods" that have been sold without published clinical proof of the claimed results.
quick.how: Home kits typically come with a skin-contact electrode, a second electrode held in the hand or placed on the body, and sometimes conductive gel. Users apply the device to areas of unwanted hair over repeated sessions, according to manufacturer instructions.
quick.risks: Skin irritation or burns from electrical current are the general concern with electrical skin devices. Product pages claim permanent results, but the only electrical method Wikipedia says the FDA recognises as permanent is needle-based electrology performed by a trained practitioner.

lead: Transcutaneous hair removal is a name for skin-surface electrical hair-removal devices, also sold as "transdermal electrolysis". They are meant to give a smooth, hairless look, particularly on the face and body, from home.[1]

Conventional electrology, practised since 1875, inserts a fine probe into each follicle and uses current to destroy the cells that grow hair.[2][1] A 1990s patent describes a non-invasive version in which a probe touches the skin without penetrating it and sends direct current through the follicles.[3]

Wikipedia places transcutaneous hair removal among methods proposed or sold without published clinical proof that they work as claimed.[1] Retail listings for home kits make permanence claims, but these are marketing statements.

chain: Electrode placed on the skin surface
Current acts at the follicle (as claimed)
angle.text: Users apply surface-electrode devices to areas of unwanted hair hoping for reduced regrowth and smoother skin, avoiding needles and clinic visits.

sections.h: Description and how it is meant to work
paras: In needle electrolysis the galvanic method makes the probe a cathode, and sodium hydroxide formed there kills the hair matrix cells, with devices delivering up to about 3 milliamperes.[2] Transcutaneous designs keep the electrode on the skin surface. A patent for surface electrolysis describes this approach, and home kits sold online include electrode patches and conductive gel.[3]

The Wikipedia hair removal article states electrology is the only permanent method recognised by the FDA, and lists transcutaneous hair removal under doubtful methods without published clinical proof.[1] Laser hair removal has been FDA-cleared since 1997 and sometimes becomes permanent after several sessions.[1]
No studies found. Searches did not find peer-reviewed clinical data for at-home surface-electrode devices; research on needle electrolysis is a separate category.

timeline.event: Charles Michel describes galvanic electrolysis for ingrown eyelashes.[2]
Laser hair removal is FDA-approved in the US.[1]
